name: Hair loss vaccine / peptides (BPC-157 for hair)

lead: BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from a protein in human gastric juice. Online posters treat it and similar peptide stacks as an experimental route to scalp healing and thicker hair.

Animal studies suggest cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects and possible faster tissue healing. Its research is mostly in laboratory animals with very limited human data, and no human hair trial was found; how it would affect follicles has not been established.

paras: It circulates in online communities as a research peptide, injected or applied, often alongside standard hair treatments, with users reporting over weeks to months.

It is not approved by any regulator for human use and has been on the WADA prohibited list since 2022. Health authorities discourage use because human safety data are insufficient, and because it promotes blood vessel growth there is concern it could affect undetected cancers.

angle.text: BPC-157 and similar peptide stacks are promoted online for scalp healing and hair regrowth, as an experimental route to thicker hair. Research on BPC-157 is mostly in animals, and no human hair-growth trial was found.

lead: BPC-157, also called Body Protection Compound 157, is a synthetic peptide of fifteen amino acids derived from a protein in human gastric juice. It was discovered by Predrag Sikirić of the University of Zagreb, with a first publication in 1993 [1]. It is not approved by any drug regulatory agency for human use [1].

Research has been mostly in laboratory animals, suggesting cytoprotective, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, while human evidence is very limited [1]. The encyclopedia article does not mention hair growth, and no human hair trial was found. Online discussion of peptide stacks for scalp claims is therefore untested.
infobox: Not approved for human use; WADA-banned since 2022 [1]

paras: No studies found on BPC-157 or peptide stacks for hair loss. Human evidence for BPC-157 in general is limited to a few preliminary safety studies, including a retrospective study of 12 patients with knee pain [1].

Health authorities discourage use because human safety data are insufficient, and the peptide's promotion of angiogenesis raises a theoretical concern about promoting cancer or enlarging undetected cancers [1]. It has been banned by WADA since 2022 under the S0 category, and some jurisdictions such as Australia and New Zealand control it as a prescription medicine [1].

timeline.event: First publication on BPC-157 by Sikirić [1].
